ut.title: Ultrasonic Thickness Testing & UT in Grand Rapids, MI
ut.description: Ultrasonic thickness gauging and UT weld inspection for Grand Rapids plants, tanks, boilers, piping and structural steel, mobilized to site. Request a quote.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) and Thickness Inspection in Grand Rapids, Michigan
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes ultrasonic testing technicians to Grand Rapids and West Michigan sites for wall-thickness surveys on tanks, vessels, boiler and process piping, plus shear-wave examination of structural and pressure welds. Send us the drawings, the governing code and a description of the access you have, and we will build the scope around it. Request a UT quote for your Grand Rapids job and we reply within one business day.

Where ultrasonic testing is used in Grand Rapids

Grand Rapids is a manufacturing metro first and a refinery or port town not at all, and that shapes what ultrasonic testing is asked to do here. The Right Place, the regional economic development group, counts more than 127,000 advanced manufacturing jobs across West Michigan, and the region is known for office furniture, automotive supply, plastics, food processing and production tooling. Each of those industries runs equipment that wears from the inside.

  • Food and beverage plants: steam headers, hot-water and glycol piping, jacketed kettles, brewing and fermentation tanks, and compressed-air receivers. Stainless vessels thin by pitting and crevice attack that a visual check cannot see.
  • Plastics and extrusion plants: steam and thermal-oil piping, hydraulic accumulators and chiller shells, many of them installed decades ago and rarely opened.
  • Furniture, tooling and metal fabrication shops: structural frames for presses and conveyors, crane runway beams, pressure vessels for paint and powder-coating lines, and welded tube assemblies.
  • Utilities and campus plants: boilers and heat exchangers at hospitals, universities and district heating loops, and natural gas distribution piping and station equipment as utilities replace aging mains.
  • Bridges and highway steel: the Grand River crossings and the interchange structures around US-131 and I-196 carry steel girders and bearings whose welded details are examined under bridge rules.

The common thread is that most of this equipment is not on a refinery inspection cycle with a full-time inspection department. It sits in plants where a maintenance manager, a plant engineer or an insurer decides when thickness gets measured. We write the scope so that it answers the question that person actually has.

What ultrasonic testing finds, and what it does not

A pulse-echo ultrasonic probe sends a short sound pulse into the material and times the echo from the far surface or from a reflector inside the wall. Thickness gauging turns that time into remaining wall. Weld examination reads the echo from planar flaws such as lack of fusion, cracks and incomplete penetration, and from volumetric flaws such as slag. Ultrasonic testing works on carbon steel, stainless steel, aluminum and many plastics, which suits the mixed materials found in a Grand Rapids plant.

It also has limits that belong in the scope document. Rough, scaled or pitted surfaces scatter sound and can hide the true back wall. Coarse-grained cast stainless attenuates the beam. Thin sections under a few millimeters may need a different probe or a different method. Corrosion that is concentrated in a small pit can be missed between grid points, so the grid spacing is an engineering decision, not a default. Linear indications that run parallel to the sound beam can be invisible to a single angle, which is why weld scans use more than one probe angle and scanning pattern. Where a question is really about surface cracking on a ferromagnetic part, the magnetic particle page for Grand Rapids is the better route.

Thickness surveys on tanks, vessels and piping

Most thickness work starts with a list of condition monitoring locations, usually shortened to CMLs. On a piping circuit those are elbows, tees, reducers, injection points and dead legs. On a vessel they are the shell courses, heads and nozzles. Our technicians mark each location, record a grid when the owner wants one, and gauge it with a dual-element probe, which handles pitted and corroded metal far better than a single-element probe.

Calibration happens on a step block of the same material before the survey and again when the probe, the temperature or the surface changes. On a hot steam line the velocity of sound in steel drops as temperature rises, so the reading is corrected, and a high-temperature probe and couplant are used rather than ordinary gel. On thin or pitted wall the gauge display is kept in A-scan view so the technician can see whether the echo is the back wall or a doubled echo. ASME Section V Article 23 carries the SE-797 practice for contact pulse-echo thickness measurement, and our guide to the thickness measurement requirements walks through the same ground in plainer terms.

Results go into a thickness table or a grid map. The owner's inspector or engineer applies the corrosion-rate and remaining-life calculation. We supply measured data that is traceable to a calibration and a procedure.

Ultrasonic examination of welds

Shear-wave examination uses an angle-beam probe, typically 45, 60 or 70 degrees, on a wedge. The technician builds a reference level or a distance-amplitude curve from side-drilled holes in a reference block, scans from both sides of the weld where access permits, and evaluates indications against the acceptance rules of the construction code. This is the method chosen when a groove weld must be examined through its full volume and a surface method cannot reach the root.

In practice, Grand Rapids work falls into three families. Structural steel under AWS D1.1 has its own ultrasonic acceptance criteria for groove welds, and bridge steel under AWS D1.5 has stricter rules for tension members. Pressure equipment under ASME Section VIII, Division 1 can call for ultrasonic examination under Mandatory Appendix 12. Process piping under ASME B31.3 can call for ultrasonic examination of welds as an alternative or an addition to other examination, with acceptance against Table 341.3.2. A procedure must name which of these governs before a probe touches steel.

Codes, the state and who owns the decision

Michigan regulates boilers and certain pressure vessels through the Department of Licensing and Regulatory Affairs, Bureau of Construction Codes, Boiler Division, and its rules adopt the National Board Inspection Code by reference for inspection, repair and alteration. The state's chief inspector and deputy inspectors inspect boilers and pressure vessels within the state's scope, and the state has said its inspectors do not perform power piping inspections under ASME B31.1, which leaves piping inspection with the owner. That detail matters for scoping: when a plant asks who decides that a B31.1 line is fit for service, the answer is the owner and whoever the owner designates.

For equipment inspected under API 510, 570 or 653, the owner's authorized inspector is responsible for the inspection. Atlantis performs the ultrasonic examination and delivers the data that inspector needs, such as thickness at CMLs or weld indications, and does not take the place of that inspector. OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119(j), the mechanical integrity element of process safety management, applies where a covered process is present. It asks for inspection and testing that follows recognized and generally accepted good engineering practice, and ultrasonic thickness data is one of the usual records offered to show it.

Who performs the work and how it is controlled

Technicians are mobilized to your site and travel to Grand Rapids for the agreed scope. Atlantis has no office in the city. The technicians are qualified under our written practice, which follows ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II technician sets up the equipment, calibrates, performs the examination and interprets the results. An ASNT Level III approves the written procedure and reviews the reports. The company is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001, which governs how records and calibrations are kept, and it describes its method in a written ultrasonic testing offer that owners can compare with their own specification.

If your own written practice or your client's contract names a different edition of the code, or an additional qualification requirement, tell us at the quote stage so the procedure can be written to it. Our Level III consulting can also review a procedure that an owner already holds.

What the report contains

A thickness report identifies each component and location, the procedure and revision, the instrument and probe, the calibration block and the temperature of the surface, the technician and qualification level, the measured value at every point, and the owner's nominal and minimum values for comparison. Weld reports add the scan plan, the probe angles, the reference level, each indication's location along the weld, its length and amplitude, and a plain accept or reject against the named criteria. Sketches and thickness grids are attached where they help the owner's engineer find the spot again years later.

Planning a UT job in Grand Rapids

Winter in West Michigan changes how ultrasonic work is planned. Lake-effect snow, wind off Lake Michigan and long spells below freezing affect outdoor tanks, rooftop equipment and bridge steel. Ordinary couplant stiffens in the cold and a probe loses contact on a frosted surface, so cold-weather work uses low-temperature couplant, surface preparation and often an enclosure or heater. Summer humidity and heat bring the opposite problem on hot lines, where the technician uses high-temperature probes and keeps the contact time short.

Outages at food, plastics and furniture plants often follow shutdown weeks tied to production cycles rather than a refinery turnaround calendar, so the schedule is usually set by the plant. Plan for badging and safety orientation, lock-out and confined-space entry where tank interiors are involved, and scaffolding or lift access where wall measurements sit overhead. Travel is by road and air through Gerald R. Ford International Airport, and we plan the mobilization around your access rules instead of promising an arrival date in advance. Surface preparation is the single biggest driver of data quality: if paint, scale or insulation is in the way, say so when you request the quote.

UT, MT or PT: choosing the method for a Grand Rapids job

Use ultrasonic testing when you need remaining wall, internal corrosion or the volume of a weld. Use magnetic particle inspection when you need surface and near-surface cracks in ferromagnetic steel, such as press frames, crane hooks or weld toes. Use liquid penetrant testing for surface-breaking flaws in stainless steel, aluminum or any non-magnetic material. Many jobs use two of the three on the same component, for example UT for the weld volume and MT for the finished surface. For comparison guidance see the ultrasonic testing guide, or the Michigan service hub at inspection services in Michigan.

Training your own technicians in Grand Rapids

Many plants prefer to keep routine thickness readings in-house and call us for weld examination or the first baseline survey. If that is your plan, our UT Level 1 and UT Level 2 courses cover theory and practice, and the ultrasonic simulator lets a trainee practice calibration and scanning before touching a part. Qualification stays with your company under its written practice, and the SNT-TC-1A eligibility checker shows the hours a candidate needs. See also our NDT training for Grand Rapids page.

faq.q: Can you gauge wall thickness on a tank or vessel that stays in service in Grand Rapids?
faq.a: Yes, in most cases. Contact ultrasonic thickness gauging works on an operating tank or pipe from the outside, provided the surface can be cleaned and the temperature is within the probe's range. We agree access, safe work conditions and the grid with your plant before the technicians are mobilized.

faq.q: How do you handle pitted or corroded surfaces when measuring thickness?
faq.a: We use a dual-element probe, calibrate on a step block of the same material, and watch the A-scan display so we can tell a true back wall from a doubled echo. Where the surface is too rough to read, we note it in the report and recommend local surface preparation instead of recording a doubtful number.

faq.q: Does ultrasonic testing replace radiography for weld examination?
faq.a: That depends on the construction code and on what the owner permits. Some codes, such as parts of ASME B31.3 and AWS D1.1, contain ultrasonic acceptance rules for production welds. The choice is agreed with the owner, the engineer and the authorized inspector before the job, so it is a scope decision, not something a technician decides on the day.

faq.q: Who decides if a thin reading is acceptable?
faq.a: The owner's inspector or engineer does. We supply measured thickness and indication data against the nominal and minimum values you give us. For API 510, 570 and 653 equipment, the owner's authorized inspector remains responsible for the inspection and applies the corrosion-rate and remaining-life calculation.

faq.q: Can you inspect stainless steel brewing and process tanks in West Michigan?
faq.a: Yes, thickness gauging works on austenitic stainless steel with the right probe and couplant, and we take care not to contaminate product-contact surfaces. Cast or coarse-grained stainless can scatter sound, so we confirm the material and the surface before quoting.

faq.q: How cold is too cold for ultrasonic work in a Grand Rapids winter?
faq.a: There is no single number, because couplant, probe and instrument each have limits. In sub-freezing weather we use low-temperature couplant, remove frost and snow from the scan surface and often add a windbreak or heater. If conditions make a reliable reading unlikely, we say so and propose a safer time window.

faq.q: What do I need to send to get a UT quote?
faq.a: Send the equipment list or drawings, the governing code or specification, the materials and nominal thickness, the surface condition, the operating temperature, any insulation to be removed and the preferred dates. A short site description with access notes helps us choose the right equipment and crew size.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office in Grand Rapids?
faq.a: No. Technicians are mobilized from our teams to your site for the agreed scope. This lets us match qualified personnel to the code and the equipment, and it means travel and access are planned with you at the quote stage rather than assumed.

faq.q: Who qualifies your ultrasonic technicians?
faq.a: Our written practice follows ASNT SNT-TC-1A. Level II technicians perform and interpret the examination, and an ASNT Level III approves procedures and reviews reports. If your contract demands a different qualification scheme, tell us when you ask for a quote so we can confirm whether we can meet it.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MPI) in Grand Rapids, MI
mt.description: Magnetic particle inspection (MPI) for Grand Rapids and Michigan castings, forgings, tooling, weldments and plant steel, mobilized to site. Request a quote.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Grand Rapids, Michigan
mt.html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes magnetic particle inspection technicians to Grand Rapids and West Michigan for castings, forgings, machined components, weldments, press frames, crane hardware and structural steel. Magnetic particle testing, also called MPI or mag particle testing, shows surface and slightly subsurface cracks in ferromagnetic steel. Send the part list, the specification and the quantity, and request an MT quote for your Grand Rapids work. We reply within one business day.

Where magnetic particle inspection is used in Grand Rapids and Michigan

Michigan search traffic for magnetic particle inspection is real and it has a recognizable shape: shops looking for someone to examine metal parts made in the state, not only plant equipment already installed. Greater Grand Rapids carries one of the highest concentrations of manufacturing jobs per head among large American metros, and the work behind that figure creates steady demand for crack detection.

  • Automotive supply parts: steering and suspension components, axle and driveline parts, brackets, fasteners and stampings made in the Tier 1 to Tier 3 supply base that stretches from West Michigan to the Ohio line. Safety-critical parts are often examined to a customer specification that names ASTM E1444 or an internal standard.
  • Castings and forgings: gray and ductile iron castings, steel castings and drop forgings come from foundries and forge shops across the state. Cracks, laps, hot tears and shrinkage that break the surface show up readily under magnetic particles.
  • Tooling and dies: West Michigan has a deep tool-and-die and production-tooling base. Tool steel dies, press components, fixtures and gages crack from heat checking and fatigue, and a die that cracks in service can ruin a production run.
  • Furniture-industry metalwork: office furniture manufacturing uses welded tube frames, steel bases, castors and stamped assemblies. Weld toes and bent tube radii are common crack sites, and customer test programs for load-bearing seating hardware lean on crack checks.
  • Material handling and plant steel: forklift masts and forks, crane hooks and hoist hardware, lifting lugs, rigging, press frames and conveyor structure.
  • Weld fabrication: pressure vessels, tanks and structural weldments built in the region's fabrication shops, examined at the final surface or after grinding.

Because the equipment is spread across so many small and mid-sized plants, we mobilize to the plant instead of asking you to ship parts away. Where a customer requires examination in a controlled bay, tell us what the bay offers when you request the quote.

What MT finds and what it misses

Magnetic particle inspection works only on ferromagnetic material, which in practice means carbon steel, low-alloy steel, tool steel, martensitic stainless and cast iron. Austenitic stainless steel, aluminum, brass and copper are not magnetic enough to be examined this way. When a component is magnetized, a crack across the field lines forces flux out of the surface. Fine iron particles gather at that leakage and mark the crack.

The method is strongest on surface-breaking cracks and gives a useful signal for slightly subsurface flaws a short way under the surface. It does not size depth, and it does not see deep internal flaws. Direction matters: a crack running parallel to the field is nearly invisible, which is why every area is examined with fields at about right angles. Coatings, heavy paint, rust and weld spatter reduce sensitivity and must be handled in the procedure. For wall thickness or internal flaws in the same part, turn to ultrasonic testing in Grand Rapids.

Technique: yokes, prods, benches and particles

Portable work on site is usually done with an electromagnetic yoke. The yoke must be able to hold a defined test weight at the largest pole spacing used, and the standard sets one lifting figure for alternating-current yokes and a higher one for direct-current and permanent-magnet yokes. We check lifting power with a certified test weight on a schedule set by the written procedure, and we record the result. Prods push current through the part and make strong fields on heavy sections, but they can leave arc burns on finished or heat-treated surfaces, so many customer specifications limit or forbid them.

Particles come in two forms. Dry powder is used on rough, hot or field-welded surfaces. Wet particles in a carrier, either visible or fluorescent, are more sensitive on finished parts. Fluorescent examination is done under UV-A light in a darkened area with the visible light level kept low. Contrast paint is used before visible particles on bare, bright steel. A pie-shaped field indicator or a shim-style indicator confirms that the field has the strength and direction needed, and the technician checks particle suspension concentration on wet-bench work.

After examination, residual magnetism can matter. Parts headed for welding, machining, precision assembly or rotating service are demagnetized, and the field is checked afterward with a gauss meter or a field indicator. Our complete guide to magnetic particle testing explains the physics in more detail.

Codes, specifications and acceptance criteria

The governing document for a MT job in this region is usually one of four. ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code Section V, Article 7, sets the method; Section VIII, Division 1 Mandatory Appendix 6 sets MT methods and acceptance for pressure vessel welds and weld repairs. ASME B31.3 at paragraph 344.3 describes magnetic particle examination of process piping with acceptance in Table 341.3.2. AWS D1.1 gives visual and MT inspection requirements for structural steel in its inspection clause, and AWS D1.5 covers steel bridge welds. For manufactured parts, the usual references are ASTM E1444 for the practice, ASTM E709 as a guide, and the customer's own drawing note. See our explainer on ASME Section V Article 7 for the main requirements.

Michigan's boiler and pressure vessel regime sits with the Department of Licensing and Regulatory Affairs, which adopts the National Board Inspection Code by reference for repairs and alterations. Where a repair weld on a boiler or vessel needs MT, the repair organization's authorization and the state's inspector set the rules. Atlantis performs the examination and reports the findings under the procedure; acceptance of a repair belongs to the party the code names. On in-service equipment covered by the API inspection codes, your own authorized inspector stays in charge of the inspection and we supply the crack data.

Who does the work

Technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope. Atlantis has no office in Grand Rapids. Personnel are qualified under the company's written practice to ASNT SNT-TC-1A: a Level II technician sets up the equipment, performs the examination and interprets indications, and an ASNT Level III approves the procedures and reviews reports. If your customer requires a particular written practice, qualification method or personnel scheme, state it in the request so the match can be checked before the job is scheduled. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001, and procedure writing can be supported through written practice development if you need your own program documented.

What the MT report contains

Each report names the component or part number and heat or lot where supplied, the procedure and its revision, the equipment, yoke lifting-power check and particle type, the technique, the surface condition, the technician and level, and the examination dates. Each indication is described by location, orientation and length, and the report states accept or reject against the specification named at the start. Photographs and sketches are added for rejectable indications, and the report records whether the part was demagnetized afterward.

Planning an MT job in Grand Rapids

West Michigan weather controls outdoor magnetic particle work more than people expect. Wet particles slow down and carriers thicken in cold air, snow and wind move powder, and fluorescent examination of field work needs shade or a booth even in daylight. Humidity affects surface condition and bright steel flash-rusts quickly after cleaning. In practice we plan outdoor jobs for dry spells, bring tents or screens, and schedule fluorescent work in a darkened area wherever possible.

In the plants, the practical questions are access and flow. Production lines in the region run on tight schedules, so we agree the sequence with your quality lead: which parts are staged, which are examined in place, and where rejected parts are tagged. Plants may require badging, safety orientation, hot-work coordination and lock-out for press or conveyor examination. Travel is by road or air through Gerald R. Ford International Airport, and we do not promise an arrival date until scope, access and qualifications are confirmed. Clean, dry surfaces free of heavy oil, scale and loose paint make the difference between a clear examination and a doubtful one.

MT, PT or UT for your Grand Rapids parts

Choose MT when the part is ferromagnetic and the concern is a surface or near-surface crack, such as on a forging, a die or a weld toe. Choose liquid penetrant testing in Grand Rapids for non-magnetic alloys, small surface checks on stainless or aluminum, or where the geometry cannot be magnetized. Choose ultrasonic testing when you need remaining wall or internal weld quality. The MT versus PT comparison sets out sensitivity, speed and limits. The national overview is at magnetic particle testing, and our state page is inspection services in Michigan.

Training your own MT technicians in Grand Rapids

Many Michigan shops examine their own production parts and need qualified people on the floor. The MT Level 1 and MT Level 2 courses build the theory and practical skill for a yoke or bench program, and magnetic particle testing training gives the overview. Qualification and certification stay with your company under its written practice. Practice questions are at NDT practice tests, and our Grand Rapids NDT training page covers the wider program.

faq.q: Do you offer magnetic particle inspection for Michigan manufacturers who make castings and forgings?
faq.a: Yes. We mobilize technicians to your plant to examine castings, forgings, machined parts and weldments in ferromagnetic steel. Send the part list, the specification or drawing note and the quantity so we can plan the equipment, the technique and the number of technicians.

faq.q: Can magnetic particle testing be done on stainless steel or aluminum?
faq.a: Only on magnetic grades. Carbon steel, low-alloy steel, tool steel, martensitic stainless and cast iron can be examined. Austenitic stainless steel, aluminum and copper alloys cannot, and liquid penetrant testing is the usual alternative for surface-breaking flaws in those materials.

faq.q: Should my Michigan parts be examined with wet fluorescent or dry powder particles?
faq.a: Wet fluorescent particles in a carrier are the most sensitive and are examined under UV-A light in a darkened area. Dry powder is used for rough, hot or field-welded surfaces where a wet carrier is impractical. The procedure and the specification decide which one applies to your part.

faq.q: Will magnetic particle inspection leave my parts magnetized?
faq.a: It can. Residual magnetism may attract chips, affect welding arcs or disturb precision assembly and bearings. When the procedure or your specification requires it, we demagnetize the part and check the remaining field with a gauss meter or a field indicator before release.

faq.q: Can you use prods on finished or heat-treated parts?
faq.a: Usually not. Prods pass current into the part and can cause arc burns that become crack starters. Many customer specifications restrict them on finished or hardened surfaces, so we plan a yoke or bench method for those parts and reserve prods for heavy weldments where they are allowed.

faq.q: Which standards govern MT work in Grand Rapids?
faq.a: It depends on the part. Pressure vessels use ASME Section V Article 7 with Section VIII Appendix 6, process piping uses ASME B31.3, structural steel uses AWS D1.1, bridges use AWS D1.5, and manufactured parts often use ASTM E1444 or a customer drawing note. We write the procedure to whichever one governs.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office or lab in Grand Rapids?
faq.a: No. We mobilize qualified technicians to your site for the agreed scope. Travel, access and badging are planned with you at the quote stage, and we confirm the qualification and equipment requirements before a start date is set.

faq.q: How do I request a quote for MT inspection in Michigan?
faq.a: Use the quote link on this page and send the component list, the governing code or customer specification, the material, the surface condition, the location and the preferred dates. We reply within one business day to confirm scope and next steps.

faq.q: Who qualifies your magnetic particle technicians?
faq.a: Personnel are qualified under our written practice, which follows ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II technician performs and interprets the examination and an ASNT Level III approves procedures and reviews reports. If your customer needs a different scheme, tell us when you ask for the quote.

pt.title: Dye Penetrant Inspection (PT) in Grand Rapids, MI
pt.description: Liquid penetrant testing for Grand Rapids stainless tanks, aluminum castings, weld repairs and machined parts, mobilized to your site. Request a PT quote.
pt.h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) in Grand Rapids, Michigan
pt.html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes liquid penetrant testing technicians to Grand Rapids and West Michigan sites to examine stainless steel vessels, aluminum castings and weldments, machined components, weld repairs and any non-porous surface where a crack could be open to the surface. Also called dye penetrant inspection, PT finds what the eye cannot. Request a PT quote for your Grand Rapids job, and we reply within one business day.

Where liquid penetrant testing is used in Grand Rapids

Greater Grand Rapids has a broad manufacturing economy, and penetrant testing is the surface method that fits the many materials that magnetic particle inspection cannot touch. The regional development group lists plastics, medical devices, aerospace and defense, food processing and production technology among its advanced manufacturing strengths, and each of them uses non-magnetic metals.

  • Food, beverage and brewing equipment: austenitic stainless vessels, tank welds, sanitary fittings, heat exchanger shells and cleanable piping. A crack on a product-contact surface is a hygiene problem as well as a structural one.
  • Aluminum and non-ferrous parts: die castings, sand castings, machined housings and fixtures. Penetrant testing is how porosity-prone aluminum is checked for surface cracks and cold shuts.
  • Weld repairs and fabrication: root and cap passes on stainless piping, buildup welds on tooling, repair welds after grinding out a defect, and fillet welds on non-magnetic assemblies.
  • Aerospace and defense suppliers: machined titanium, nickel and aluminum components where customer specifications call for surface inspection. Atlantis offers penetrant examination as an ASNT SNT-TC-1A-based service and works to the specification the customer names.
  • Plastics and process plants: molds, screws, barrels and tooling made from tool steel and alloys, plus stainless process piping and pressure vessels.
  • Medical-device and precision manufacturing: small stainless and titanium machined parts that are cleaned and examined as lots.

The work often sits inside an existing production flow, so the practical value of a mobilized technician is that the parts do not leave your plant and the schedule stays under your control.

What PT finds and what it misses

Liquid penetrant testing finds only discontinuities that are open to the surface. A penetrant with low surface tension is applied to a clean, dry part and given time to be drawn into any crack, lap, seam, cold shut or pore. After the excess is removed, a developer draws the trapped liquid back out so the defect appears as a visible mark. It works on steel, stainless steel, aluminum, titanium, nickel alloys, brass, copper and many ceramics, ferrous or not.

It will not detect a flaw that is closed at the surface by smeared metal, shot peening, heavy machining or paint. It will not see subsurface flaws at all. Porous materials give false indications everywhere. Cleaning, not the dye, decides the outcome: oil, scale, flux or coating left in a crack keeps the penetrant out. For internal flaws and thickness, ultrasonic testing in Grand Rapids is the route, and for ferromagnetic parts magnetic particle inspection is often faster and more sensitive to shallow tight cracks.

Technique: from precleaning to final inspection

A penetrant job runs in a fixed order: precleaning, application of penetrant, a dwell time, excess removal, developer, and examination. Precleaning removes grease, paint and scale by solvent, detergent or mechanical means; peening, grit blasting and some wire brushing can smear metal over a crack, so the procedure controls them. Penetrants are classed by dye type, with fluorescent examined under UV-A light and visible-dye penetrants examined in white light, and by removal method: water-washable, post-emulsified, or solvent-removable. On site, the solvent-removable visible process is the standard choice because it needs no wash station. Fluorescent systems give more sensitivity where a darkened area is available.

Dwell time depends on the material, the flaw type and the temperature, and it is written into the procedure. After removal of the surface excess, a thin even coat of developer is applied, usually a non-aqueous wet developer on field work, and the part is examined during a development time. Parts for stainless and nickel alloys, and for some titanium, also call for control of halogen and sulfur content in the materials, because contaminants can attack the metal. Written procedures follow ASME Section V Article 6 and ASTM E165, and the explainer on Article 6 shows how those requirements fit together.

Temperature, light and the Michigan calendar

Article 6 expects the part and the penetrant materials to sit between roughly forty and one hundred twenty-five degrees Fahrenheit unless the procedure has been demonstrated for a different range. West Michigan winters leave outdoor steel well below that window for months, and a hot summer day can push a dark stainless tank above it. A cold part makes the penetrant sluggish and the developer slow to dry; a hot part makes the penetrant evaporate before the dwell is complete. When conditions fall outside the window we warm or shade the area, or qualify the procedure for the range as the code allows, rather than accept doubtful results.

Light matters too. Visible-dye work needs good white light on the surface, and fluorescent work needs a darkened area with a UV-A source that is checked before use. Humidity can affect how quickly developer dries, and wind carries solvent and overspray, so tent or screen the work area on outdoor stainless and tank repairs.

Weld repairs and stainless fabrication in practice

Much of the penetrant work in a manufacturing metro comes from repair and fabrication rather than from new-build pressure vessels. A cracked tooling insert is ground out, rewelded and checked before it goes back into a press. A stainless tank seam is dressed after a leak and examined before the vessel is returned to service. An aluminum housing is machined and checked for cracks before it moves to assembly. In each case the technician examines the original defect area after grinding to confirm that the crack has been removed, and then examines the finished weld. Skipping the first step is a common reason for a repair weld that fails again in service, because a crack tip left in the base metal simply grows through the new weld.

Where the material is a nickel alloy or a stainless grade with strict contaminant limits, we ask for the product certificate of the penetrant materials and keep it with the report. Where parts are wiped after examination, the cleaning agent and the final rinse are chosen so that no residue is left on surfaces that later receive plating, coating or food contact.

Codes and acceptance criteria

For pressure equipment, the method comes from ASME Section V Article 6 and the acceptance rules come from the construction code: Section VIII, Division 1 Mandatory Appendix 8 gives liquid penetrant methods and acceptance for vessel welds, and ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.4 sets liquid penetrant examination of process piping against Table 341.3.2. Structural weldments use AWS D1.1 for visual and surface inspection requirements, and manufactured parts commonly follow ASTM E165 or a customer drawing note that sets the acceptance limits, often by indication type and size.

In Michigan, boilers and pressure vessels fall under the Department of Licensing and Regulatory Affairs and its boiler rules, which adopt the National Board Inspection Code for inspection, repair and alteration. When a repair weld on a vessel or boiler needs a penetrant check, the repair organization and the inspector the rules name decide acceptance. Atlantis performs the examination and delivers the record. For equipment under API 510, 570 or 653, the owner's authorized inspector is the inspector of record and receives our data.

Who does the work

What the PT report contains

The report lists the component or lot, material and surface condition, the procedure and revision, the penetrant system with product batch numbers, the dwell and development times, the surface temperature, the light levels used, the technician and level, and the date. Each indication is located, measured and classified as linear, rounded or relevant, and the report states accept or reject against the named criteria. Photographs of rejectable indications are included where useful, together with notes on any repair and re-examination.

Planning a PT job in Grand Rapids

Tell us the surface finish, the alloy, the access and whether cleaning solvents are restricted at your site. Food and beverage plants may restrict chemicals, require food-safe cleaning after examination and expect a written sanitation plan; medical and aerospace customers may control the penetrant brand and the post-clean steps. We plan for those limits from the quote stage. Allow time for surface preparation, because machining, grinding and blasting must be done before the penetrant goes on, and for post-examination cleaning of both the part and the surrounding area.

We do not promise a start before those details are in hand. Scheduling around production shifts, shutdown weeks and lock-out requirements is normal on this kind of job.

PT, MT or UT for your job in Grand Rapids

Use PT when the metal is non-magnetic, when the shape is awkward for magnetizing, or when you want a simple surface check on a weld repair. Use MT when the part is ferromagnetic and you want the most sensitivity for tight cracks. Use UT when the question is remaining wall or the inside of a weld. The MT versus PT comparison is a short way to decide, and the national overview is at penetrant testing. For other work, see inspection services in Michigan.

faq.q: Can liquid penetrant testing be used on stainless steel brewing and food-processing equipment?
faq.a: Yes. Penetrant testing is the normal surface method for austenitic stainless steel, which cannot be examined by magnetic particles. We control the materials and the post-examination cleaning so the product-contact surfaces are left clean, and we follow your site's rules on chemicals.

faq.q: What kinds of flaws can dye penetrant testing find?
faq.a: It finds cracks, laps, seams, cold shuts and porosity that are open to the surface. It cannot find flaws that are closed at the surface or that lie below it, and it is unreliable on porous materials. Careful cleaning before the test decides how well it works.

faq.q: Why does temperature matter for a penetrant test?
faq.a: ASME Section V Article 6 expects the part and the penetrant materials to be inside a set range unless the procedure is demonstrated for a wider one. Cold parts slow the penetrant and the developer, and hot parts dry the penetrant too quickly, so results can be missed or become hard to read.

faq.q: Is fluorescent or visible penetrant better for field work?
faq.a: Visible, solvent-removable penetrant is the usual field choice because it needs no wash station or darkened area. Fluorescent penetrant is more sensitive and is used where a dark area and a UV-A source are available. The procedure and the specification set which type applies.

faq.q: Can you examine aluminum castings and machined parts?
faq.a: Yes, penetrant testing works well on aluminum and other non-ferrous alloys. We discuss the surface finish, since machining or blasting can smear metal over a crack, and agree the cleaning and etching steps with you before the job is scheduled.

faq.q: Which standards govern PT in Michigan plants?
faq.a: Pressure vessels and piping use ASME Section V Article 6 with Section VIII Appendix 8 or B31.3, structural steel uses AWS D1.1, and manufactured parts often follow ASTM E165 or a customer drawing note. We write the procedure to the document your contract names.
